docs.text: Chapter 2 Groups and Vector Spaces 2.2 Groups 2.2.4 Lagrange’s Theorem Lemma 2.26 Every coset of H in a group G has the same number of elements. Proof : Let the coset be a * H . Then we can make an one-to-one mapping between a * H and H : f : a * H \longrightarrow H, a * h \longrightarrow h So a * H has the same number of elements as H . \square Lemma 2.28 The distinct cosets of H in a group G are disjoint. Proof : Assume a * H and b * H are 2 distinct cosets of H , assume c \in a * H \cap b * H , then we can find h_1, h_2 such that a h_1 = c = b h_2 , so we have a h_1 h_2^{-1} = b , so b \in a * H . That means a * H = b * H . Then we reach a contradiction. \square Theorem 2.29 (Lagrange’s theorem) Let G be a group of finite order and let H be a subgroup of G . Then the order of H divides the order of G . That is, |H| divides |G| . Proof : Just apply Lemma 2.26 and Lemma 2.28. \square 2.2.5 Induced Operations; Isomorphism Definition 2.36 Let ⟨G,*⟩ be a group, H a subgroup and let S = \{H_0 = H,H_1,H_2, ...,H_M \} be the set of cosets of H in G . Then the induced operation between cosets A and B in S is defined by A * B = C \text{ if and only if } a * b= c for any a ∈ A, b ∈ B and some c ∈ C , provided that this operation is well defined. The operation is well defined if for every a ∈ A and b ∈ B, a * b ∈ C ; there is thus no ambiguity in the induced operation. Theorem 2.38 If H is a subgroup of a commutative group ⟨G,*⟩ , the induced operation * on the set of cosets of H satisfies (a * b) * H = (a * H) * (b * H). Furthermore, the operation is well defined. Proof : We will prove it's well defined, Let a_1 \in a * H, b_1 \in b * H , we want to show (a * b) * H = (a_1 * b_1) * H Since a_1 \in a * H , we have a_1 = a h_1, h_1 \in H . Similarly, we have b_1 = b h_2, h_2 \in H . Since G is commutative, a_1 b_1 = a h_1 b h_2 = (ab) (h_1h_2) . Since H is a subgroup, h_1 h_2 \in H . So we have (a * b) * H = (a_1 * b_1) * H Then the operation is well defined. \square
